content: Lignite, commonly known as brown coal, represents the lowest rank of coal and is predominantly utilized as a fuel source for steam-electric power generation. It is characterized by its brownish-black appearance and a notably high inherent moisture content, which can reach up to 66%. Additionally, it contains a significantly higher ash content compared to bituminous coal. Structurally, lignite is a heterogeneous mixture of compounds, and no single structural formula can adequately describe its composition. The energy content of lignite ranges from 10 to 20 MJ/kg (equivalent to 9 to 17 million BTU per short ton) on a moist, mineral-matter-free basis. This includes both its inherent moisture and mineral matter. When lignite reacts with quaternary amines, it forms a compound known as amine-treated lignite (ATL). ATL is commonly employed in oil well drilling fluids to minimize fluid loss during drilling operations. Due to its low energy density, lignite is inefficient to transport and is not widely traded on the global market compared to higher-grade coals. Instead, it is often combusted in power stations located in close proximity to lignite mines, such as those in Australia’s Latrobe Valley. Power plants that burn lignite typically emit significantly higher levels of carbon dioxide compared to plants that utilize black coal. The continued operation of lignite-fired power plants, especially when combined with strip mining and in the absence of emissions-reducing technologies like carbon sequestration, remains a politically contentious issue.
